chapters.title: Chapter 4: Cross-Sectional Momentum - Ranking and Rotation

lessons.title: The Jegadeesh-Titman Momentum Effect: The Academic Foundation

children.text: Jegadeesh and Titman's 1993 study has been mentioned throughout this course as the origin of momentum research. This lesson goes further: how the study was actually built, why its methodology became the template nearly every momentum strategy since has followed, and how a finding that started as an academic curiosity ended up as a standard, named risk factor sitting alongside market, size, and value in modern asset pricing models.

body.text: Jegadeesh and Titman didn't test one momentum strategy, they tested a whole grid of them, varying both the formation period and the holding period, and found the effect held up across nearly all of it. That robustness, not any single number, is why the finding was taken seriously enough to eventually become its own standard factor in academic finance.

children.text: The Original Methodology: A Grid of Formation and Holding Periods

Rather than testing a single formation period and a single holding period, Jegadeesh and Titman built strategies across every combination of J-month formation periods, 3, 6, 9, and 12 months, and K-month holding periods, also 3, 6, 9, and 12 months, producing 16 separate J-month/K-month strategies in total, each one ranking US stocks into deciles by trailing return and going long the top decile, short the bottom. The most frequently cited single result from the paper is the 6-month formation, 6-month holding strategy, often shorthanded as the 6/6 strategy, but the paper's real strength was that the effect showed up, in broadly similar magnitude and statistical significance, across nearly the entire grid, not just one favorably chosen combination.

body.caption: The formation/holding grid concept (illustrative representation, not the paper's exact reported figures)

body.label: The 6/6 strategy's headline result
body.context: The most commonly cited figure from the original 1965-1989 sample: buying the top decile of 6-month past winners and shorting the bottom decile of 6-month past losers, held for 6 months, produced roughly 1% per month of excess return, before transaction costs

children.text: From Anomaly to Factor: Carhart's Four-Factor Model

markDefs.definition: Mark Carhart's 1997 extension of the Fama-French three-factor model, adding a momentum factor, commonly labelled UMD or WML, to explain systematic return patterns tied to recent price performance.

children.text: The finding's real graduation from anomaly to established factor came in 1997, when Mark Carhart added momentum as a fourth factor to the Fama-French three-factor model, originally built from market risk, size, and value, to better explain differences in mutual fund performance. This factor, usually labelled UMD, up minus down, or WML, winners minus losers, is built the same way SMB and HML are: a long-short portfolio, in this case long recent winners and short recent losers, whose return isolates the momentum effect specifically.

body.caption: Carhart's four-factor model: a portfolio or fund's excess return, explained by its exposure to the market, size, value, and momentum factors, with alpha left over as whatever the four factors cannot explain.

children.text: This mattered practically, not just academically. Once momentum became a standard factor, fund analysts could check whether a manager's outperformance was genuine skill, alpha, or simply a hidden tilt toward recent winners that would have shown up in any momentum-loaded portfolio. Quant desks, including in India, now routinely check a strategy's factor exposures, market, size, value, and momentum, before crediting a result to genuine edge.
Does It Survive Publication? Out-of-Sample Evidence

Chapter 1 covered the limits to arbitrage that let a public anomaly survive. Momentum offers real evidence for this: follow-up academic research studying anomalies before and after their original publication has generally found that most documented anomalies weaken noticeably once traders start exploiting them, yet momentum has been found to hold up better than most, continuing to show significant returns in samples well after 1993, and in dozens of other countries and asset classes it was never originally tested on. This does not mean momentum is immune to decay, most researchers do find some reduction in raw magnitude over time, but its persistence has been unusually strong relative to other published anomalies.

The academic literature has been honest about momentum's weaknesses too. The raw 1% per month figure is before transaction costs, and shorter formation and holding combinations, higher turnover strategies by design, give back a meaningful share of that return to trading costs in practice. Some of the effect's strength has historically come from smaller, less liquid stocks, exactly the names where real-world execution costs and capacity constraints bite hardest. And momentum carries the crash risk covered in Chapter 1's case study, a well-documented tendency toward sharp, sudden reversals that a simple average monthly return figure does not capture. None of this invalidates the finding, but a serious quant reading the original paper should read past the headline 1% figure to these caveats before assuming the strategy is straightforward to run at scale.

body.text: Notice how much of this lesson connects back to earlier ones: the crash risk from Chapter 1, the transaction cost warnings scattered through Chapters 2 and 3, and the market-neutral, long-short construction from Chapter 4's opening lesson. The academic foundation isn't separate from the practical mechanics, it's the rigorous version of exactly the same ideas.

body.title: What made the original study convincing?
body.question: Why was Jegadeesh and Titman's 1993 finding taken more seriously than a single lucky backtest on one formation and holding period combination might have been?
options: Because they only tested one strategy and it happened to work well
Because the effect held up, in broadly similar magnitude, across all 16 combinations of formation and holding periods they tested
Because the paper was published in a well-known journal, regardless of its actual results
Because momentum has never had a losing period since 1993
body.explanation: The robustness across the full grid of 16 formation/holding combinations, not any single favorable pairing, is what made the finding credible rather than looking like a data-mined result specific to one arbitrary choice of parameters.

body.title: Evaluating a fund manager's momentum exposure
body.scenario: A mutual fund has beaten its benchmark by 4% a year for five years. When you run its returns through Carhart's four-factor model, the fund shows a large, statistically significant positive loading on the UMD factor, and its alpha, once that exposure is accounted for, is close to zero.
body.prompt: Based on this lesson, what does this result suggest about the source of the fund's outperformance?
body.modelAnswer: It suggests the fund's outperformance is largely explained by a structural tilt toward recent winners, a momentum factor exposure, rather than genuine stock-picking skill. Since the alpha, the return left over after accounting for the fund's exposure to market, size, value, and momentum, is close to zero, the manager isn't beating a momentum-adjusted benchmark, they are essentially riding the same well-documented momentum factor this lesson describes. This is exactly the kind of check factor models were built to enable: separating a real, skill-based edge from a known, systematic tilt that could be replicated cheaply.

body.label: Explore published factor return data via Kenneth French's data library
body.description: Kenneth French's publicly available data library, widely used in academic and industry research, includes historical momentum (UMD) factor returns alongside market, size, and value, a genuine primary source for anyone who wants to study the effect's history directly.

cards.definition: Jegadeesh and Titman's methodology of testing momentum across every combination of several formation periods and several holding periods, rather than a single chosen pair.
The momentum factor added to the Fama-French model by Carhart in 1997, built as a long-short portfolio of recent winners minus recent losers.
Carhart's asset pricing model, extending Fama-French's three factors, market, size, and value, with a fourth factor, momentum, to better explain fund and portfolio returns.
The portion of a portfolio's return left unexplained after accounting for its exposure to known systematic factors like market, size, value, and momentum, commonly used as a measure of genuine skill.

points: Jegadeesh and Titman tested momentum across a full grid of 16 formation/holding period combinations, and the effect held up across nearly all of them, which is what made the finding credible.
The most cited headline figure, the 6-month formation, 6-month holding strategy, produced roughly 1% per month of excess return before transaction costs in the original sample.
Carhart's 1997 four-factor model formalized momentum into a standard factor, UMD or WML, now used industry-wide to separate genuine investment skill from a simple systematic momentum tilt.
Momentum has shown unusually strong persistence after publication compared to most other documented anomalies, though not complete immunity to decay.

Serious caveats remain: transaction costs eat into the raw return figure, the effect is stronger among less liquid stocks, and the strategy carries real crash risk, all reasons to treat the headline 1% figure as a starting point for further scrutiny, not a guaranteed return.
